newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close range bound as mkt awaits data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close range bound as mkt awaits data.

text.p: The prices of U.S. government securities closed little changed Wednesday as market participants had little new information upon which to trade.

Most players already have discounted a 25-basis-point hike in short-term interest rates when the Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on May 20. Last Friday's nonfarm payrolls report contained signs of incipient wage inflation and Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has noted in the past that he would be vigilant in watching wages, thus increasing expectations of another tightening.

Trading volume of 10-year notes was higher than normal, said Maureen Mooney, senior analyst at GovPX. At 1230 EST/1630 GMT) trading volume of 10-year paper was 80 percent higher than normal. Mooney said heavy corporate issuance could have been the reason this happened as hedging activity in the 10-year sector may have been higher than normal.
J.C. Penney (JCP.N) issued a $2.5 billion corporate debt offering in six tranches.
Mooney added that volume at the long end of the maturity spectrum had been higher than at the short end in the past couple of sessions.

"We're in a pattern. Claims might give us a little bit of a clue (on Thursday)," said Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. But any significant price movement was unlikely before Friday's data, she said.
Stephensen said there was a fair chance the Fed would tighten again on May 20 due to the continuing pressure seen on wage inflation that surfaced in last Friday's monthly nonfarm payrolls report.
"It seems every report we get is suggestive of a stronger economy," Stephensen said.

Mark Vitner, economist in the capital markets group at First Union Corp, said rumors had started to circulate that rising air fares could lead to a sharper-than-expected increase in the consumer price index due next week, with CPI rising perhaps as much as 0.5 percent.
Vitner said a strong CPI reading could upset the notion that strong growth was continuing with low inflation.
"This will probably be against the majority view, but we see the Fed moving only two more times," Vitner said.
He also expected to see strong retail sales as Easter sales would be included in the March total.
"It seems we're just stuck once again. We have no real news to trade on unless one of the Fed governors says something," said Stephen Slifer, chief economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
Slifer expected the levels of bond prices would remain range bound until Friday when March retail sales and producer prices would be released.
"I don't know why or how we backed up, but we're back to pre-employment (payrolls) levels," said Slifer.
The bond market has been characterized by little price movement all week amid a dearth of economic news.

The Treasury's 30-year bond closed off 1/32 at 94-03 to yield 7.10 percent. The 10-year note closed down 2/32 at 95-13/32, yielding 6.90 percent. The five-year note traded off 1/32 at 99-14/32 to yield 6.76 percent. The two-year note closed unchanged at 99-22/32, yielding 6.42 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum the three-month bill was down one basis point at 5.09 percent; the six-month bill was up one basis point at 5.35 percent and the year bill was unchanged at 5.63 percent.
